bibliography.abstract: Due to climate change and urbanisation, urban heat islands (UHIs) and heatwaves are increasingly impacting cities in summertime around the world, including less studied Scandinavian cities. Local cooling effects from waterbodies and tall vegetation exist with large geographical variations, and their dynamics need further attention for understanding their abilities to cool during heatwaves. This study investigates turning points of waterbody cooling effects in coastal Copenhagen (Cfb) on three specific June dates covering a heatwave in 2018, a windier but warm and moist day in 2019, and a colder but moist day in 2020. Significant and consistent cooling effects were found for all three summers, from coastal sea (3.92-4.91◦C; 195 m), lakes (1.54-1.96◦C; 225 m), especially lakes larger than 4.68 ha (2.81-3.27◦C; 165-285 m) and lakes more compact in shape (size/perimeter ≥0.0053ha/m) (2.61-3.35◦C; 315-375 m). The smaller but significant cooling trends for lakes within proximity to tall vegetation (0.63-1.21◦C; 135-225 m) together with observed significantly lower land surface temperatures surrounding this subset of lakes (–0.6-0.8◦C) indicate two supplementary but equally important ways for mitigating heat – increasing cooling through larger urban waterbodies and lowering land surface temperatures with tall vegetation. The cooling intensities were lowest on the windy date in 2019, but highest in 2020, indicating limited but significant cooling intensities of dry heatwave waterbody cooling.
bibliography.title: Comparing waterbody cooling during heatwave with subsequent summers in high-latitude coastal Copenhagen

en.caveats: The findings are based on observations from only three specific days, which may not capture the full seasonal or interannual variability of waterbody cooling dynamics.
en.what: This study measured the land surface temperature cooling effects of coastal seas and lakes in Copenhagen across three June days in 2018, 2019, and 2020, capturing a dry heatwave, a windy warm day, and a cooler moist day. The coastal sea provided 3.92–4.91°C of cooling up to 195 meters away, while lakes larger than 4.68 hectares cooled their surroundings by 2.81–3.27°C up to 285 meters. Lakes surrounded by tall vegetation showed smaller direct cooling extents but had significantly lower surrounding land surface temperatures of -0.6 to 0.8°C.
en.why: It quantifies how the cooling performance of urban blue infrastructure changes under different meteorological conditions, demonstrating that while waterbody cooling intensity is lowest during windy conditions and constrained during dry heatwaves, combining larger waterbodies with tall vegetation offers a dual pathway for urban heat mitigation.
